report:
Conclusion: the claim “soursop cures cancer in humans” is unsupported and should be treated as false. Soursop/graviola (*Annona muricata*) contains acetogenins that can kill or slow cancer cells in test-tube and animal studies, and reviews describe plausible mechanisms—but they also emphasize that clinical trials in humans are lacking or inadequate, so lab findings cannot be equated with a cure (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9497149/). Cancer Research UK states plainly that graviola is promoted as an alternative cancer treatment but “there is not enough reliable evidence that it works as a treatment for cancer,” and warns that online claims rely on unsupported opinion and anecdotes (https://www.cancerresearchuk.org/about-cancer/treatment/complementary-alternative-therapies/individual-therapies/graviola). Memorial Sloan Kettering likewise notes antitumor effects in laboratory/animal models but no proven human cancer benefit, plus possible side effects and drug interactions (https://www.mskcc.org/cancer-care/integrative-medicine/herbs/graviola).

There is also a safety concern: annonacin, a major soursop acetogenin, is a mitochondrial complex-I inhibitor linked epidemiologically and experimentally to atypical, levodopa-resistant parkinsonism in Guadeloupe (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18816693/). Eating the fruit occasionally as food is different from using concentrated extracts as treatment. Anyone with cancer should not replace surgery, radiation, chemotherapy, immunotherapy, or clinical trials with soursop; discuss supplements with an oncology clinician because “natural” does not mean safe or effective.
